title: Minestrone alla genovese
subtitle: Ligurian vegetable soup finished with pesto
excerpt: A full-bodied Ligurian minestrone with French beans, potatoes, courgettes, and pasta, finished with a generous spoonful of fresh basil pesto stirred in just before serving. Thicker, greener, and more aromatic than a standard minestrone.
sourceNotes: Minestrone alla genovese is a classic of Ligurian cooking, documented in Pellegrino Artusi's La Scienza in Cucina e l'Arte di Mangiar Bene (1891, public domain) and in multiple twentieth-century Ligurian cooking references including the work of Paolo Lingua (La Cucina dei Genovesi, 1989). The defining element is the stirring of fresh basil pesto into the finished soup.

recipe.freezeNotes: Not suitable for freezing once the pesto is added. The base soup (without pesto or pasta) can be frozen.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Add pasta and pesto per portion at serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The soup base can be made the day before. Add pasta for the last 10 minutes of reheating, and stir in pesto just before serving.

content.text: Minestrone alla genovese is distinguished from other minestrones by the spoonful of basil pesto stirred in at the very end. The pesto does not cook; it hits the hot soup and its basil and garlic aromas bloom immediately. The soup is fuller-bodied than a standard minestrone, with small pasta shapes and potatoes giving it weight, and the pesto makes it smell intensely of summer.

items.prepNote: trimmed and cut into 2 cm pieces
ditali, ditalini, or small elbow macaroni

content.text: Use the freshest pesto you can find or make it yourself: the basil pesto entry in this library has the full recipe. Jarred pesto can substitute but will give a less vivid result.
Heat the olive oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion, celery, and carrot and cook for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft.

Add the potato, courgette, and green beans. Stir to coat in the oil. Pour in the stock. Bring to the boil and simmer for 20 minutes until the vegetables are just tender. Add the borlotti beans and simmer for 5 more minutes.
Add the pasta and cook for the time given on the packet, or until just tender. Taste and season the soup generously.
Remove from the heat. Stir in the pesto. Serve immediately in warm bowls with grated Parmesan and a drizzle of olive oil.

items.symptom: Pesto loses its bright colour and tastes flat
items.cause: Added to a boiling soup or stirred in too far ahead
items.fix: Remove the soup from the heat before adding the pesto. The residual heat is enough.

content.text: Minestrone alla genovese is the soup of Liguria, the narrow coastal strip between the Apennines and the Ligurian Sea. It is the home of both pesto and of some of the most characteristic Italian vegetable cooking. The Ligurian preference for olive oil, basil, pine nuts, and Parmesan runs through everything. Adding a spoonful of pesto to the minestrone just before serving is one of those Italian culinary rules so obvious and so good that it is worth learning by heart.
